previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of systolic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, COPD, and alcohol dependence was re-admitted for worsening shortness of breath and volume overload due to medication non-compliance and heavy alcohol use. He presented with dyspnea, abdominal swelling, and cough, and was found to have elevated proBNP, mild pulmonary congestion on chest X-ray, and signs of fluid retention. He received IV furosemide and was monitored for alcohol withdrawal. An ultrasound showed an echogenic liver and splenomegaly, raising concern for early cirrhosis. Despite medical advice, he left against medical advice on hospital day two, still volume overloaded. He was discharged on his baseline heart failure medications with strong counseling to adhere to treatment and avoid alcohol.

# Atypical chest pain: Patient presented with acute onset of 
chest pain and dyspnea that was initially concerning for ACS. 
However patient with no ischemic EKG findings and negative 
troponin x 2. He has a history of chronic pain for which he has 
been followed by his cardiologist Dr. ___. His pain has 
typically not been responsive to nitroglycerin which he received 
in ED without significant relief. We considered PE or dissection 
but thought these were less likely without tachycardia, 
pleuritic pain, or radiation of pain to back. Patient was well 
appearing with stable vital signs. Potentially secondary to 
edema or respiratory complaints. Patient reported several 
episodes of chest pain during his admission for which he 
received additional EKGs without signs of ischemia or right 
heart strain. Patient felt that this pain was similar to his 
chronic pain. We managed his pain with tylenol and oxycodone 
with symptomatic improvement. He had resolution of this chest 
pain upon discharge.

# Atrial fibrillation: Patient has a history of atrial 
fibrillation on rivaroxaban. He was in fibrillation throughout 
most of his admission. His admission was notable for episodes of 
tachycardia (150s-170s), usually while walking to bathroom, that 
were likely RVR (___). We restarted his home metoprolol. 
Patient had previously been on metoprolol and it was unclear if 
this had been stopped by outpatient providers or whether patient 
had self discontinued this due to lack of understanding of his 
medications. He tolerated the metoprolol well and was discharged 
on Metoprolol Succinate XL 50 mg PO DAILY and his home xarelto.

# Acute on chronic decompensated Systolic Congestive Heart 
Failure: Patient has history of systolic CHF with LVEF ___, 
who presented with dyspnea on exertion and rest after his 
medications were stolen. His exam was notable for crackles and 
wheezing as well as elevated JVP. He received a chest x-ray 
(___) with evidence of pulmonary edema. He was diuresed with 
80 mg IV Lasix with good output. During his admission his exam 
improved with diminished crackles and return to euvolemia. His 
weight decreased from 99.6 kg to 97.9 kg with diuresis. He was 
discharged on his home 60 mg torsemide QD.

#Acute Kidney Injury
The patient developed mild ___ thought to be secondary to IV 
diuresis with creatinine of 1.3 on day of discharge. Patient 
instructed to follow up with PCP and to have this rechecked upon 
follow up.

# COPD: Patient presented with wheezing on his exam. This was 
not thought to be COPD exacerbation but rather due to inability 
to take home COPD medications. He received albuterol and 
ipratropium nebulizers as well as his home COPD medications. His 
exam improved significantly with no wheezes upon discharge. 

# EtOH abuse: Patient is a daily vodka drinker and had his last 
drink prior to admission. He does not have a history of 
withdrawal seizures. Upon admission he was placed on a CIWA and 
was given 2 mg Ativan for scores>10. He received folate, 
thaimine, and multivitamin. He did well during his admission 
with intermittent complaints of headache, nausea and anxiety 
with an exam that showed mild tremor. The patient had continued 
withdrawal at time of discharge with CIWA score of 10 though 
left against medical advice. He recounting understanding of the 
risk of leaving the hospital prematurely. He denied history of 
withdrawal seizures however. 

# Mouth abscess: Patient presented with painful swelling of left 
lower oral cavity. Patient denied trauma but has poor dentition. 
 Patient was started on clindamycin in ED but then switched to 
augmentin upon admission to the floor. He received an incision 
and drainage in the ED. This was thought to be odontogenic 
abscess in the setting of poor dentition. OMFS was consulted to 
evaluate abscess and felt that patient could benefit from 
additional drainage and underwent ___ I&D with OMFS (___). 
Panorex (___) showed near edentulous dentition, 2 areas of 
possible lucency. Patient was instructed to follow up with OMFS 
in clinic for removal of fractured teeth and to complete a 7 day 
course of augmentin. 

# Left toe abrasion: Patient presented with complaint of pain on 
the left foot. His exam showed an 1 cm ulcerated base with 
crust, without significant erythema or fluctuance around the 
lesion. Given lack of systemic findings such as fever or white 
count, this was not thought to be cellulitis. X-ray of the foot 
did not show fracture or evidence of osteomyelitis. There was no 
drainable collection on exam. We cleaned and monitored the 
wound, which was stable to improved upon discharge. He was 
discharged with a short course of oxycodone for his chronic left 
foot pain from his amputation. 

CHRONIC/RESOLVED:
# Lactic acidosis: Patient had elevated lactate to 2.8 
(___) up from 1.6 prior admission (___). This was 
initially concerning for potential systemic hypoperfusion. 
Patient has known infection in oral cavity however other sources 
are possible. Repeat lactate to 2.4. Given his history of poor 
cardiac function, cardiogenic shock is possible although he 
appears to be well perfused. He was discharged in stable 
condition.

Home
 
Discharge Diagnosis:
Primary: 
Acute on chronic decompensated systolic congestive heart failure
Secondary: Atypical chest pain, Atrial fibrillation, Oral 
abscess, COPD, Alcohol withdrawal

 
Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Clear and coherent.
Level of Consciousness: Alert and interactive.
Activity Status: Ambulatory - Independent.

 
Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you here at ___ 
___. You came to the hospital because you 
had chest pain and difficulty breathing. You received multiple 
EKGs and tests of your heart enzymes that did not show signs 
that you were having a heart attack. We think that this was 
probably your chronic chest pain. Your shortness of breath was 
likely caused by your lack of your outpatient medications. We 
gave you nebulizers and your home medications to help your COPD. 
We also gave you medicines to help remove the excess fluid from 
your lungs and body. Your breathing improved during you 
admission and you were discharged on your home medications.  

During your hospital admission, you had a few episodes of a very 
fast heart rate due to your atrial fibrillation. We restarted a 
medication (metoprolol) that can help your atrial fibrillation. 
When you came to the hospital you also had a large swollen area 
of your mouth. We thought this was an oral abscess and you 
received two procedures to help drain the swelling. You were 
given antibiotics (augmentin) for this as well which you should 
continue after discharge. You showed signs that you were 
withdrawing from alcohol and we treated you with ativan as 
needed. 

You should have close follow up with your primary care physician 
for your COPD. It is very important that you follow up with your 
cardiologist for your heart condition, atrial fibrillation and 
chest pain, and report any weight gain or difficulty breathing. 
You should follow up with your oral surgeon for your mouth 
abscess and any further dental evaluation or procedures. 

We recommended that you stay in the hospital longer because of 
ongoing alcohol withdrawal symptoms but you chose to leave the 
hospital. Please make sure you follow up with all of your 
appointments below. 

We wish you the best,

Your ___ care team
